'''''Agave americana''''', [[Common name|commonly known]] as the '''century plant''',<ref name="BSBI07">{{BSBI 2007|access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''maguey''', or '''American aloe''',<ref>Bailey, L.H.; Bailey, E.Z.; the staff of the Liberty Hyde Bailey Hortorium. 1976. ''Hortus third: A concise dictionary of plants cultivated in the United States and Canada''. Macmillan, New York.</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] [[species]] belonging to the family [[Asparagaceae]]. It is [[Native plant|native]] to Mexico and the United States, specifically Texas. This plant is widely cultivated worldwide for its [[Ornamental plant|ornamental value]] and has become [[Naturalized species|naturalized]] in various regions, including Southern California, the West Indies, South America, the Mediterranean Basin, Africa, the Canary Islands, India, China, Thailand, New Zealand and Australia.<ref name="Irish">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/agavesyuccasrela0000iris |url-access=registration |title=Agaves, Yuccas, and Related Plants: A Gardener's Guide |first=Gary |last=Irish |publisher=Timber Press |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-88192-442-8 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/agavesyuccasrela0000iris/page/94 94]–97}}</ref>

Despite being called "American aloe" in common parlance, ''Agave americana'' is not closely related to ''[[Aloe]]'' species.

==Description==
The common name "century plant" stems from its [[monocarpic]] nature of flowering only once at the end of its long life. After flowering, the plant dies but produces [[Basal shoot|adventitious shoots]] from the base, allowing its growth to continue.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-4053-3296-5|pages=1136}}</ref> Although it is called the century plant, it typically lives only 10 to 30 years.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UO1MecufH00 |title=Century Plant brings excitement to Bucknell's greenhouse |date=2023-01-05 |last=WNEP |access-date=2024-05-25 |via=YouTube}}</ref> It has a spread around {{convert|6-10|ft|m|1|order=flip|abbr=on}} with gray-green leaves measuring {{convert|3-5|ft|m|1|order=flip|abbr=on}} in length, each with a prickly margin and a heavy spike at the tip that can pierce deeply. Towards the end of its life, the plant produces a tall, branched stalk adorned with yellow blossoms, which can reach a height of {{convert|25|–|30|ft|m|0|abbr=on|order=flip}}.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

==Naming==
The species was given its [[binomial name]] ''Agave americana'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in the first edition of ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753). This name is the one still in use today.<ref name="GRIN"/>

==Cultivation==
''A. americana'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], particularly valued for its large, dramatic mature form. It is often found in modernist, [[xeriscapes]] ([[Drought-tolerant plant|drought-tolerant]]), and desert-style [[Cactus garden|cactus gardens]]. It is popularly used in hot climates and areas prone to drought.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AGAM |title=''Agave americana'' (American century plant) |work=Native Plant Database |access-date=2013-06-11 }}</ref> The plant's presence can evoke the ambiance of 18th- to 19th-century [[Spanish colonial]] and Mexican provincial areas in the Southwestern United States, California, and [[xeric]] regions of Mexico. In dry beach gardens in Florida and coastal areas of the Southeastern United States, it is a favored choice for landscaping.{{citation needed|date=June 2013}}

When grown as a houseplant, ''A. americana'' is tolerant of light levels ranging from direct sunlight to shade, and requires minimal watering. It undergoes a winter resting period at temperatures around {{convert|10 to 12|C||sp=us}}. It thrives in a highly porous, sandy potting soil, should be allowed to dry out between waterings, and should be repotted annually in the spring.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chiusoli |first1=Alessandro |last2=Boriani |first2=Luisa Maria |title=Simon & Schuster's guide to houseplants |date=1986 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |location=New York |isbn=0-671-63131-4}}
</ref>

===Subspecies and varieties===
The [[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] recognizes two [[subspecies]] and two [[variety (botany)|varieties]] of ''A. americana''. Additionally, there are several [[Cultivar|cultivars]], including 'Marginata,' 'Mediopicta,' 'Mediopicta Alba,' 'Mediopicta Aurea,' 'Striata,' and 'Variegata.' Some of these cultivars, along with the parent species, have received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].

==Uses==
[[File:ToolsIxtleMAPHidalgo.JPG|thumb|Tools used to obtain agave's [[ixtle]] fibers, at the [[Museo de Arte Popular, Mexico City|Museo de Arte Popular]], Mexico City, D.F.]]

===Cuisine===
''Agave americana'' has various uses starting in [[pre-Columbian Mexico]]. If the [[flower stem]] is cut before flowering, a sweet liquid known as ''[[aguamiel]]'' ("{{Lit|honey water}}) can be collected from the plant's hollowed heart. This liquid can be [[fermented]] to produce the alcoholic drink called ''[[pulque]]'' or ''[[octli]]'' used in pre-Columbian Mexico.<ref name="HLAW">{{Cite book|title=Handbook to Life in the Aztec World|last=Dr. Aguilar|first=Moreno|publisher=California State University|year=2006|isbn=0-8160-5673-0|location=Los Angeles|pages=371, 318|url=https://archive.org/details/handbooktolifein0000agui/page/371}}</ref>

In the tequila-producing regions of Mexico, agaves are known as ''mezcales''. [[Mezcal]] refers to the high-alcohol product obtained through fermented agave distillation, and ''A. americana'' is among the several ''[[Agave]]'' species used for this purpose. The specific mezcal known as [[tequila]] is produced from ''[[Blue agave|Agave tequilana]]'', commonly referred to as "blue agave." Mezcal comes in various types, some of which may be flavored with the intensely pungent [[mezcal worm]].<ref>{{cite web |first1=Barbara |last1=Hansen |date=June 21, 2011 |title=Escamoles & Maguey Worms: John Sedlar on the Joy of Eating Bugs |work=L.A. Weekly |url=http://www.laweekly.com/restaurants/escamoles-and-maguey-worms-john-sedlar-on-the-joy-of-eating-bugs-2374680 }}</ref>

Mezcal and tequila, despite being produced from agave plants, differ from pulque in their sugar extraction techniques and classification as [[distilled spirits]]. In mezcal and tequila production, the sugars are obtained by heating the piñas (or hearts) of the plants in ovens, as opposed to collecting aguamiel from the cut stalk of the plant. Therefore, if pulque were to be distilled, it would not be classified as mezcal but rather as a distinct beverage.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barbezat |first=Suzanne |date=2017-08-28 |title=Tequila, Mezcal and Pulque |work=TripSavvy |url=https://www.tripsavvy.com/tequila-mezcal-and-pulque-1588785 |access-date=2018-07-25}}</ref>

Agaves are also found throughout Latin America and are used in similar ways. In Ecuador, the equivalent of ''pulque'' is known as ''[[guarango]]'', which has recently been distilled as [[Miske (drink)|''miske'']]. Its use in making fermented and distilled drinks may have been a reason why settlers introduced the plant to Spanish [[Alta California]], and according to reports made to ethnologist [[J. P. Harrington]], [[Chumash people|Chumash]] consultants had seen a mission priest collect juice from the stalks, though the Chumash themselves did not produce alcoholic beverages.<ref name=":92">{{Cite book |last=Janice |first=Timbrook |title=Chumash Ethnobotany: Plant knowledge among the Chumash people of southern California |collaboration=[[Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History]] |publisher=[[Heyday Books|Heyday]] |year=2007 |isbn=9781597140485 |edition=1st |location=Berkeley, California |pages=22 |oclc=77011598}}</ref> 

[[Agave nectar]] is marketed as a [[natural sweetener]] with a [[Low glycemic index diet|low glycemic index]], primarily due to its high [[fructose]] content.<ref>{{cite web |last=Oudhia |first=P. |year=2007 |title=Agave americana L. |url=https://www.prota4u.org/database/protav8.asp?h=M4&t=Agave,americana&p=Agave+americana |work=[[Plant Resources of Tropical Africa]] |access-date=2017-07-04 |archive-date=2017-12-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171226131052/https://www.prota4u.org/database/protav8.asp?h=M4&t=Agave,americana&p=Agave+americana }}</ref>

=== Fibers ===
The leaves of ''A. americana'' yield [[Fiber plant|fibers]] called ''pita'', which are suitable for making ropes, nets, bags, sacks, matting, and coarse cloth. They are also used for leather embroidery in a technique known as ''[[piteado]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hulle |first1=Ashish |last2=Kadole |first2=Pradyumkumar |last3=Katkar |first3=Pooja |title=Agave Americana Leaf Fibers |journal=Fibers |date=March 2015 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=64–75 |doi=10.3390/fib3010064 |language=en |issn=2079-6439|doi-access=free }}</ref> Both pulque and maguey fiber played significant roles in the pre-Columbian economy of Mexico.<ref name="HLAW"/> In California, where the plant was introduced during Spanish colonization, the fibers began to be used by indigenous people like the [[Chumash people|Chumash]] to make string as an alternative to the shorter fibers of native ''[[Hesperoyucca whipplei]]''; the fiber cordage was employed in making string, sewing shoes, and possibly for basketry handles. In Morocco, fibre from ''A. americana'' has also been described in materials-science literature as [[Sabra (textile)|sabra fibre]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ouarhim |first1=Wafa |last2=Essabir |first2=Hamid |last3=Bensalah |first3=Mohammed-Ouadi |last4=Rodrigue |first4=Denis |last5=Bouhfid |first5=Rachid |last6=Qaiss |first6=Abou el kacem |year=2019 |title=A Comparison between Sabra and Alfa Fibers in Rubber Biocomposites |journal=Journal of Bionic Engineering |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=754–767 |doi=10.1007/s42235-019-0061-0}}</ref><ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last=Janice |first=Timbrook |title=Chumash Ethnobotany: Plant knowledge among the Chumash people of southern California |collaboration=[[Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History]] |publisher=[[Heyday Books|Heyday]] |year=2007 |isbn=9781597140485 |edition=1st |location=Berkeley, California |pages=26 |oclc=77011598}}</ref>

===Medicine===
''Agave americana'' contains [[agavasaponins]] and [[agavosides]] (fructans).<ref>{{cite news|title=List of All Chemicals - Agave americana (Agavaceae)|url=https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/plants/report/60.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170125173741/https://phytochem.nal.usda.gov/phytochem/plants/report/60.pdf|archive-date=January 25, 2017}}</ref> It is used in [[traditional medicine]] to treat various ailments,<ref>{{cite book|title=Aztec Medicine - Aztec Student Research Guide|author=Thomas H. Frederiksen|year=1997–2005|url=https://ambergriscaye.com/pages/mayan/aztecmedicine.html}}</ref> and as a [[laxative]], [[diuretic]], and [[diaphoretic]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Agave americana|publisher=Arizona State University|url=https://www.public.asu.edu/~camartin/plants/Plant%20html%20files/agaveamericana.html}}</ref> In California, following its introduction, it was reported that despined leaves were split and made into a [[poultice]] for boils.<ref name=":92" /> However, a comprehensive review of research literature using systematic methods ([[scientific review]]) did not find sufficient data to support its effectiveness or safety.<ref>{{cite news|title=Agave (Agave americana): an evidence-based systematic review by the Natural Standard Research Collaboration|year=2006|doi=10.1080/J157v06n02_09|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/6618763}}</ref> ''A. americana'' can cause severe [[allergic dermatitis]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Contact dermatitis from Agave americana|year=2005 |doi=10.1016/s0001-7310(05)73128-8|pmid=16476291 |last1=de la Cueva |first1=P. |last2=González-Carrascosa |first2=M. |last3=Campos |first3=M. |last4=Leis |first4=V. |last5=Suárez |first5=R. |last6=Lázaro |first6=P. |journal=Actas Dermo-Sifiliograficas |volume=96 |issue=8 |pages=534–536 }}</ref>

===Heraldry===
The plant holds [[heraldic]] significance and is featured in the [[coat of arms]] of Don Diego de Mendoza, a Native American governor of the village of [[Ajacuba]], [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]].<ref>[http://home.pacbell.net/nelsnfam/mexico.htm pacbell.net/nelsnfam/mexico] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706180805/http://home.pacbell.net/nelsnfam/mexico.htm |date=July 6, 2008 }}</ref>

===Art===
Additionally, the [[Aztecs]] used the pulped leaves of ''A. americana'' to create paper.<ref name="HLAW" /> The fragments known as the [[Humboldt fragments]] were made using this technique.<ref name="WAM">{{cite book |last1=Mason |first1=William A. |title=A History of the Art of Writing |date=1920 |publisher=The Macmillan co. |page=114 |url=https://archive.org/details/historyofartofwr00maso/page/114/mode/1up }}</ref>
